chunks: What are brushes?. The question: What are brushes?
Brushes are the stationary contacts of a brushed motor. They are small blocks, usually carbon, pressed by springs against a spinning ring of copper segments called the commutator.
They do two jobs: they carry current from the fixed terminals into the spinning coils, and they help flip the current in each coil at the right moment.
Picture a pencil lead pressed against a spinning bicycle rim. The lead stays still, the rim slides past it, and the lead stays in contact.
In the motor, the rim is the commutator and the pencil lead is the brush, carrying electricity instead of marking paper.
The analogy has one gap: the brush also has to switch from one copper segment to the next, which a pencil never does.
End view of a 6-segment commutator. Brushes (green, static, spring-loaded) touch segments 2 and 5.
Each armature coil is connected between two adjacent segments, so the coils form two parallel paths from the + brush to the minus brush (one round each side of the ring).

As the ring turns, each brush briefly bridges two adjacent segments, shorting the coil between them while it passes the neutral axis; after 60° the brushes sit on the next pair of segments and that coil has moved into the other path, so its current has reversed.
Brush: a stationary conductor, often carbon, that slides on the commutator. Commutator: copper segments on the rotor, each wired to a coil. Rotor: the spinning part of the motor.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage a carbon brush loses as current passes through it, roughly 0. 5–1 volts per brush.
Brushless motor: a motor that switches current electronically instead.
Take one wire loop spinning between magnets, with its ends on two half-rings and two fixed brushes touching the half-rings.
Half a turn later, each brush has slid onto the other half-ring, so the current in the loop reverses. That reversal keeps the push in the same direction.
The brushes also waste a little voltage. Take the top of the usual range, 1 volts per brush: the current passes through two brushes, so 2 volts is lost.
At 2 amps, that is 2 volts times 2 amps = 4 watts . That is the whole idea: brushes bring in power and flip the current.
"Brushes are the stationary conductive contacts, usually carbon, spring-pressed against the commutator on the rotor.

They feed current from the motor terminals into the spinning windings, and together with the commutator's segments they reverse the current in each coil at the right angle, so the torque stays in one direction.
The trade-off is that they wear, drop about a volt, create friction and spark slightly, which makes noise. Brushless motors avoid this by switching electronically."
